definition: In computer vision, the Kanade–Lucas–Tomasi (KLT) feature tracker is an approach to feature extraction.
details: It is proposed mainly for the purpose of dealing with the problem that traditional image registration techniques are generally costly. KLT makes use of spatial intensity information to direct the search for the position that yields the best match. It achieves faster speed than traditional techniques by examining far fewer potential matches between the images.

explainer.lead: A computer vision approach to feature extraction that uses spatial intensity information to find the best match quickly. It matters because it avoids the high cost of traditional image registration.

tiers.eli5: Instead of checking every possible spot to see where a point moved, it uses the surrounding brightness pattern to guess where to look.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply KLT to track features across frames by examining far fewer potential matches; a pitfall is that the speed comes from that directed search, so tracking quality depends on the local intensity information being informative.
tiers.paperLevel: Definition: use spatial intensity information to direct the search for the position yielding the best match, achieving faster speed than traditional techniques by examining far fewer potential matches between images. Known limit: it is proposed mainly to deal with the costliness of traditional image registration, so it trades exhaustive matching for a guided search.

explainer.example: Tracking a corner across two video frames, KLT searches only near the expected position rather than across the whole image.
